ideas.canonical_en: The Great Molasses Flood of Boston in 1919
ideas.question: Ek shehar mein sirop ki lehar aayi aur sadkon par tabahi macha di, ye sach hai?
ideas.hook: Ek din Boston ki sadkon par meetha sirop ki lehar aayi, aur 21 log mar gaye.
ideas.angle: A funny-sounding setup with a dark ending, plus the physics of why cold syrup is deadly.

ideas.canonical_en: Why do you suddenly need to pee more when it's cold?
ideas.question: सर्दी में बार-बार पेशाब क्यों लगता है, जबकि पानी भी कम पीते हैं?
ideas.hook: सर्दी में पानी कम पीते हो, फिर भी बाथरूम के चक्कर क्यों बढ़ जाते हैं?
ideas.angle: Cold diuresis: the body is not pushing out extra water. It is protecting your core by moving blood around.

ideas.canonical_en: Why shooting stars are mostly the size of a grain of sand and what makes them glow
ideas.question: Why does a grain of sand light up the whole night sky?
ideas.hook: That streak across the sky? It's usually a speck the size of a grain of sand.
ideas.angle: Meteors glow because of air compressed in front of the grain, not friction. Tie it to the Leonid meteor shower, which peaks around Nov 17-18.

ideas.canonical_en: Why do the Leonid meteor showers sometimes turn into meteor storms with thousands of shooting stars per hour?
ideas.question: Why did the sky once rain 100,000 meteors an hour, and could it happen again?
ideas.hook: In 1966, the night sky over Arizona rained about 40 meteors every single second.
ideas.angle: Covers the comet's dust trails and the 33-year cycle behind the rare Leonid storms (1833, 1966, 1999-2002), not how a shooting star glows. It's timed to this week's peak on Nov 17-18.

ideas.canonical_en: Why does a glacier in Antarctica bleed blood-red water?
ideas.question: Why is there a glacier in Antarctica that looks like it's bleeding?
ideas.hook: In Antarctica there's a glacier that bleeds. And the 'blood' comes out clear.
ideas.angle: The red is not algae, as explorers once guessed. It is very salty, iron-rich water from a lake that has been sealed under the ice for over a million years. The water comes out clear and only turns red when it meets air, the same way iron rusts. Microbes live down there in total darkness by 'breathing' iron.

ideas.canonical_en: Why the scariest pirate in history may never have killed anyone until his last fight
ideas.question: Did Blackbeard actually kill anyone, or was the smoking beard the whole trick?
ideas.hook: The most feared pirate in history set his own beard on fire, and that may be why he never had to kill anyone.
ideas.angle: Blackbeard as a branding genius. It was psychological warfare: slow-burning fuses under his hat and a terrifying image, so ships surrendered without a fight. Historians find no reliable record of him killing anyone before his final battle on November 22, 1718.

ideas.canonical_en: How could a whale sink a whaling ship on purpose (the Essex, Nov 20, 1820)?
ideas.question: How did a whale sink a ship on purpose?
ideas.hook: This week in 1820, a whale looked at a ship, swam away, turned around and rammed it. Twice.
ideas.angle: This uses the anniversary to explain the whale's head. Its front third is a giant oil-filled sonar organ sitting on top of the 'junk', a stack of tissue that works like a shock absorber. Studies suggest males may use it as a battering ram on each other.

ideas.canonical_en: Why did America have two different Thanksgivings in 1939?
ideas.question: How did one country end up eating Thanksgiving dinner on two different Thursdays?
ideas.hook: In 1939, America had two Thanksgivings, one week apart.
ideas.angle: The cause was not religion or tradition. It was shopping. November 1939 had five Thursdays, retailers feared a short Christmas season, and FDR moved the holiday. States split, families split, and the joke name was 'Franksgiving'.

ideas.canonical_en: Did tulip mania really bankrupt the Dutch, or is the famous bubble mostly a myth?
ideas.question: Did the famous tulip bubble really make people go broke?
ideas.hook: History's craziest bubble bankrupted nobody we can find.
ideas.angle: A versus of the legend and the archives. The legend, popularized in an 1841 book: chimney sweeps trading houses for bulbs, then the whole country ruined. The archives, as historian Anne Goldgar found: buyers were mostly wealthy merchants, she found no bankruptcy caused by tulips, and the real damage was broken promises and reputations. Prices really did spike and crash in Feb 1637.

ideas.canonical_en: Why do scam emails seem deliberately badly written and unbelievable?
ideas.question: If scammers want your money, why are their emails so obviously fake?
ideas.hook: That terrible scam email is a genius filter.
ideas.angle: Flips the usual 'scammers are dumb' joke. A 2012 Microsoft Research paper argues that the silly story is a sieve: anyone who replies to something that absurd has already screened themselves in as an easy target, so the scammer doesn't waste hours on skeptics.

ideas.canonical_en: How a gold duplication glitch can make a whole game world poor (hyperinflation shown in a blocky town)
ideas.question: What happens to a game world when one player can copy unlimited gold?
ideas.hook: He found a glitch that made him infinitely rich. It made him poor.
ideas.angle: Inflation explained through a real, repeated game disaster: Diablo III's 2013 auction-house gold duplication bug, Diablo IV's trade dupe, and New World switching its whole economy off. It is retold as an original blocky-town story, so viewers watch prices change brick by brick instead of hearing an abstract economics lesson.

ideas.canonical_en: The first Ponzi scheme was built on a real, legal trick with postage coupons, so why did it become a fraud?
ideas.question: What was Charles Ponzi actually pretending to do with people's money?
ideas.hook: The world's most famous scam began with a trick that actually worked.
ideas.angle: Everyone knows the word 'Ponzi', but almost nobody knows the stamps. Postal reply coupons were cheap in war-torn Europe and could be swapped for pricier US stamps, which is real arbitrage. Ponzi promised 50% in 45 days. Doing the trade would have meant moving mountains of paper coupons, so he paid old investors with new investors' money instead. Auditors later found only about $30-60 worth of coupons.

ideas.canonical_en: Why did a bottle of Coca-Cola cost exactly 5 cents from 1886 to about 1959, through two world wars and the Depression?
ideas.question: How did one soda keep the same 5-cent price for seventy years while every other price went up?
ideas.hook: For seventy years, inflation couldn't touch one soda.
ideas.angle: Three physical traps kept the price stuck. In 1899 the company agreed to sell syrup to bottlers at a fixed price with no end date (reportedly partly to get two lawyers out of the office). It painted '5 cents' on walls all over the country. And by 1950 it owned most of the US vending machines, which only took a nickel. The company even asked the Treasury for a 7.5-cent coin. Shown as a generic red soda with no logo.

ideas.canonical_en: Why did a store that stopped faking discounts lose almost a billion dollars in one year (JCPenney 2012)?
ideas.question: Why did shoppers abandon a store the moment it stopped faking its sales?
ideas.hook: A store stopped lying about prices. Its customers ran away.
ideas.angle: Instead of the usual 'stores trick you' story, the honest store is the one that gets punished. The video shows the anchoring effect through a real business that tested it at full scale, just before Black Friday week.

ideas.canonical_en: How did one trader borrow millions against tanks of salad oil that were mostly water, and why did almost nobody notice when it collapsed in November 1963?
ideas.question: How do you borrow millions against oil you don't have?
ideas.hook: A man borrowed millions on salad oil that didn't exist.
ideas.angle: This is a heist with no break-in. Inspectors dipped a tube into each tank, but hidden compartments kept a thin layer of real oil right where they measured, with water or nothing below. Banks lent against warehouse receipts, the receipts were backed by those tanks, and the tanks were fake. The scandal broke on Nov 19, 1963, and three days later JFK was shot, so it fell to the back pages. The anniversary is this week.

ideas.canonical_en: In 1958 the Hope Diamond was sent from New York to the Smithsonian in a plain brown package by registered mail, for $2.44 in postage.
ideas.question: Why would anyone mail the world's most famous diamond like a birthday card?
ideas.hook: The world's most famous diamond was mailed for two dollars forty-four.
ideas.angle: This is security psychology shown as a story. Armed guards and armoured cars announce 'something valuable is here'. A dull brown parcel announces nothing. The real lesson is that being boring can be the best disguise.

ideas.canonical_en: Why are there now more $100 bills in existence than $1 bills?
ideas.question: You almost never see a hundred-dollar bill, so why are there more of them than ones?
ideas.hook: There are more hundreds than ones.
ideas.angle: A versus format: the $1 bill wears out in a wallet, while the $100 hides under mattresses and in vaults worldwide. Up to about 80% of $100s are estimated to be outside the US, used as a 'safe' savings currency.

ideas.canonical_en: Why D.B. Cooper's $200,000 ransom was almost impossible to spend, and why only $5,800 of it has ever been found
ideas.question: D.B. Cooper got away with $200,000. So why did almost none of it ever show up?
ideas.hook: America's most famous hijacker got away with money he couldn't spend.
ideas.angle: Today is the 55th anniversary (Nov 24, 1971). Instead of asking who he was, we follow the money: before handing it over, the FBI and Seattle First National Bank photographed the serial number of every one of the 10,000 twenty-dollar bills on microfilm, so every bill was traceable.

ideas.canonical_en: Why does an Italian bank keep hundreds of thousands of wheels of Parmesan in its vaults as loan collateral?
ideas.question: Why does a real bank lend money against wheels of cheese?
ideas.hook: This bank's vault is full of cheese, not gold.
ideas.angle: Since 1953, the Italian bank Credem has accepted Parmigiano Reggiano as collateral. A cheesemaker has to wait two years for the cheese to age before they can sell it, so the bank lends them cash now and ages the wheels in its own warehouse. It's a real lesson in how collateral works.

ideas.canonical_en: Why did India once print a special rupee that was only allowed to be spent outside India, in the Gulf (1959)?
ideas.question: India ने 1959 में ऐसा रुपया क्यों छापा जो सिर्फ Dubai, Qatar और Kuwait में चलता था, India में नहीं?
ideas.hook: एक ज़माने में Dubai की करेंसी Indian रुपया थी।
ideas.angle: Most people have never heard of the Gulf rupee. The 'oh, THAT's why' is gold smuggling: Indian rupees in the Gulf were swapped for gold, the gold was smuggled into India, and the rupees came home and drained India's foreign exchange. So India printed a different-coloured rupee that couldn't come back.

ideas.canonical_en: Why did India have to fly its own gold to London in 1991, in boxes it had to borrow?
ideas.question: 1991 में India को अपना सोना London क्यों भेजना पड़ा, और boxes भी उधार क्यों लेने पड़े?
ideas.hook: 1991 में India ने अपना सोना plane में भरकर London भेज दिया।
ideas.angle: Most videos stop at 'India almost went bankrupt'. This one follows the actual gold: about 47 tonnes sent in four batches in July 1991, the gold boxes borrowed from the Bank of England, the van that broke down in Mumbai, and why the lenders wanted the gold kept outside India. It explains what pledging means (it was a loan, not a sale) and stays out of politics.

ideas.canonical_en: How did two prospectors in 1872 fool top bankers and a leading New York jeweler with a field 'full of diamonds' they had planted themselves?
ideas.question: How did two miners convince America's richest men that diamonds were lying on the ground?
ideas.hook: Two miners found a field of diamonds. They'd planted every one.
ideas.angle: The Great Diamond Hoax of 1872, told as a mechanism explainer: how you 'salt' a field, why a famous jeweler's appraisal made the con look certain, and how one geologist exposed it in November 1872 by noticing gems in places nature could never put them. It's a near-anniversary, and much less overdone than the usual famous cons.

ideas.canonical_en: How did a broke Boston man who was laughed at for shipping ice to the tropics end up selling ice in Calcutta, and why did it not melt on the way?
ideas.question: चार महीने का समुद्री सफ़र, गर्मी 35 डिग्री, फिर भी बर्फ़ कलकत्ता पहुँची कैसे?
ideas.hook: उसने बर्फ़ बेची... गर्मी से तपते कलकत्ता को।
ideas.angle: Indian connection: the 1833 ship Tuscany reached Calcutta with about 100 of its 180 tons of ice still frozen. The mechanism is sawdust insulation, and a big block melts slowly. Before that, his first shipment melted in Martinique and Boston papers mocked him. That gives the full formula of stupid idea, laughter, worse, right all along.

ideas.canonical_en: When its only bank failed in 1931, a small town printed its own money on thin sheets of wood, so why did almost nobody cash it back in?
ideas.question: What do you do when your town's only bank locks its doors with everyone's savings inside?
ideas.hook: When the bank kept their money, a town made its own out of wood.
ideas.angle: A Depression-era bank failure seen from one small town. The Chamber of Commerce let depositors trade up to 15% of their frozen savings for scrip printed on thin cedar and spruce. Collectors and tourists wanted the wooden bills as souvenirs, so most were never redeemed, and the Chamber later bought the failed bank's building.

ideas.canonical_en: How did a man in a fake officer's uniform announce that Napoleon was dead in 1814, send London stock prices soaring for one morning, and drag a naval war hero into the scandal?
ideas.question: How much is one fake message worth on the stock market?
ideas.hook: Napoleon died in 1814. For about one morning.
ideas.angle: The first great fake-news stock scheme, 200 years before social media. A messenger in a red uniform arrives in Dover saying Napoleon is dead, bond prices shoot up, and the conspirators sell what they bought a few days earlier. By the afternoon it all falls apart. The twist is that one convicted man, a famous navy captain, may have been innocent.

ideas.canonical_en: Why did paying a bounty for every rat killed in 1902 Hanoi end with people farming rats?
ideas.question: सरकार ने हर मरे चूहे के पैसे दिए, तो शहर में चूहे और क्यों बढ़ गए?
ideas.hook: सरकार ने चूहे मारने के पैसे दिए, और चूहे बढ़ गए।
ideas.angle: This is the documented version of the famous 'cobra effect'. Historian Michael Vann found the records. The twist is that the Delhi cobra story Indian viewers know cannot be proven, but this one can.

ideas.canonical_en: Why is the biggest shopping day called Black Friday, and why is the 'stores finally get in the black' explanation a later rewrite?
ideas.question: Why is the biggest shopping day of the year named after something dark?
ideas.hook: Black Friday was named by people who hated it.
ideas.angle: Almost everyone repeats the 'in the black' profit story. The documented origin is Philadelphia traffic police dreading the day-after-Thanksgiving crowds by the early-to-mid 1960s. Merchants hated the name and pushed 'Big Friday', which flopped. Decades later, around the late 1980s, retail took over the name with the friendlier accounting story. Published two days before Black Friday 2026.
